newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Korea's Midopa says safe from takeover.
newsitem.headline: Korea's Midopa says safe from takeover.

text.p: South Korea's Midopa Department Store Co said on Monday it was confident it could stave off any hostile takeover bid but some securities analysts questioned its defence.

"Midopa is safe from any corporate raider," said spokesman Chun Byung-sam of Dainong Corp, parent company of Midopa Department Store, South Korea's leading department store chain. "We see no problem at all."
Midopa came under the spotlight on Thursday when Shindongbang Corp and Korea Industrial Co told the Korea Stock Exchange they were considering a take over.

The presidents of Korea Industrial and Shindongbang are brothers. Midopa operates a flagship store in Seoul's most fashionable shopping district and has 20 distribution outlets throughout South Korea.
If successful, it would be the first major hostile takeover in South Korea.
"We already control 40 percent of shareholders' votes in Midopa. It is very easy for us to secure an additional 10 percent support," said Dainong's Chun without elaborating.
Midopa's shares fell by a daily limit of eight percent, or 3,000 won ($3.4), to 35,200 won on Monday after soaring to a 1997 high of 47,500 won last week.
"The talk of the hostile takeover has been diluted on the market as some investors believe it is unrealistic," said analyst Hwang Chang-joong of LG Securities.
But some other brokers said small trading volume of 83,000 shares meant many investors were still holding on in anticipation of the joint takeover bid being successful.

Security analysts, particularly those from foreign brokerage houses, said the bid was likely to be an opening salvo by corporate predators. The government has scrapped a 10 percent ceiling on individual stock holdings in listed companies.

"This rings an alarm bell for every Korean company that they should pay more attention to business performance and stock prices," said Kim Min-tae, senior economist at Daewoo Research and Economic Institute.

But local newspapers said South Korea's major chaebol, or conglomerates, had joined forces to try to thwart the hostile takeover. Institutional investors affiliated with the top three chaebol bought all 50 billion won worth of bonds with warrants issued by Midopa last Friday.
Dainong and a underwriter denied the speculation.
"It's groundless we are a white knight for Midopa," said Kim Sang-ki, director of Samsung Life Insurance, an affiliate of the Samsung Group.
A white knight is a potential friendly acquirer sought out by a company for protection from a hostile takeover.
The bonds with warrants give the holder the option to buy a specified number of the issuer's shares at a set price within a certain time period.
"We bought the bonds for investment purposes," Kim Sang-ki said. "Midopa is undervalued asset-rich stock. We can exercise warrants to buy Midopa shares at 30,000 won over three years from July."
In return, Samsung Life Insurance also expected more insurance contracts from Midopa, he added.
The bond issue could not help Midopa defend an early takeover bid as warrants could be exercised only after July.

"The bond issue has no significant meaning. There seems to be no quick way to defend a hostile takeover bid, if there is any attempt," said Kim Min-tae, senior economist at Daewoo Research and Economic Institute.
"Midopa's takeover is likely," an analyst at a Western brokerage firm said. "More hostile takeover attempts will follow." ($1 = 869.50).
